output.quote: Ok so then we need something in the DAG to cause interviews. My original idea was that during design review, gaps that the human needs to answer should be flagged in the review, and that would stale the design, and require interview to fix it. Could that work simply?
output.summary: Approved G1026 design revision 6 after five review rounds (round 5 approved, no open findings). Reviews flag `owner question:` findings (always material, only when undoing a wrong choice reaches outside the goal or changes product behaviour/direction and no option clearly dominates); design blocks for an interview; the owner's words are recorded verbatim; the frontier is unchanged (option b): the re-review resolves the question against human_decisions now carried on review/filter cards; card.shrink blobs the unclipped human_decisions list; approve items and the PR body show human decisions. It follows the owner's idea that review gaps needing the human should stale the design and require an interview.

responses.review_tests:1:3: fixed: the node set is now stated precisely. An approve item for node X reads every graph node that is not a descendant of X ({m for m in nodes if X not in graph.ancestors(m)}), and the PR body reads every node that is not a descendant of the op writing it. In the shipped graph: approve_design reads its ancestors (nothing runs beside it), approve_merge reads its ancestors plus integrate (all but merge), and the PR body written by integrate reads integrate's ancestors, integrate itself and approve_merge (all but merge), so integrate's own answers appear there; integrate rewrites the body on each run, so the run after the answer lists it. Why this rule: it is the smallest one that passes the frozen tests and still names no node. Plain ancestors miss nodes that run beside the item. 'The whole goal history for approve_merge' would make the engine pick out the final approval by name or by a new rule. Leaving out descendants is one existing graph query, the same for every approve node and the PR body, and it keeps approve_design free of earlier-round downstream op answers (e.g. integrate's 'Rebase it?') after a reopen (D2). Merge answers come after the last approval, so no approval could show them anyway. Frozen tests: none change; test_an_answered_integrate_question_is_listed_with_kind_op already expects the integrate entry on approve_merge, and the approve_design and PR-body assertions hold because their answers are on design. Also fixed the reviewer's note: a filter card's subject is graph.subject(n) or graph.filter_subject(n) (shipped filter nodes have no review.subject), in D5, §5, §6 and the revision-5 3:2 note. Changed sections are listed in the revision-7 note.

output.summary: Revision 7 keeps revision 6 and answers review_tests 1:3. Approve items now read human_decisions over every node of the goal's graph that is not a descendant of the item's node, and the PR body over every node that is not a descendant of the op writing it. In the shipped graph approve_design reads its ancestors, while approve_merge and the PR body read every node except merge, so answered integrate questions are listed (the PR body includes integrate's own answers). Review and filter cards keep 'subject and its ancestors', with the subject defined as graph.subject(n) or graph.filter_subject(n). No frozen test changes.

findings.text: human_decisions on cards has no shrink step. D5 and §5 say entries are unclipped on cards and 'shrink turns it into a blob view if needed'; the frozen decisions_of helper also expects a blob view after shrink. But the shipped card._steps (card.py, around line 420) and SPEC 3.14's shrink rule (SPEC.md:1581) can blob only prompt, instructions, inputs/context/policy entries, correction texts and candidates/notes. A top-level human_decisions list is never a candidate. §9 'Card size' also says the list 'is clipped', which contradicts D5. Revision 5 adds the list to all six review and filter cards, which already carry an unshrinkable previous.findings (this review's own card is 7,367 canonical bytes). Fix: in §5, add a card.py shrink step that blobs a top-level human_decisions list (key summary 'N items'). In §6, add it to SPEC 3.14's shrink order. Correct §9 to 'not clipped on cards; shrink blobs it'. Add a test: with a long answer, the review_design card's human_decisions becomes a view that decisions_of reads back.

output.summary: Revision 6 resolves 4:1, and the r5-to-r6 diff touches only the areas it lists. Checked against card.py on 25186a5: the two-element step needs its own _apply branch, and the design adds one. _blob on a list gives the 'N items' key summary and indented JSON that the frozen decisions_of can read back. The blobbed value is no longer a candidate, and shrink runs last in build. SPEC 3.14's list and §9 are now consistent with D5. No new findings.

findings.text: test_cards_carry_the_instruction_and_stay_within_the_limit cannot pass after implementation: it abandons the review_design and adversary_design leases and then calls until_ready(g, 'review_impl'); on read_dev abandon makes a node reclaimable and the Pilot's plain start is refused with not_ready 'the lease expired; pass --reclaim' (reproduced with the same sequence on read_dev; hidden today because the test stops at line 363). Implement cannot fix a frozen test. Fix: finish the review runs (card, _ = self.p.run(g, node)) and check those cards, or restart with --reclaim.

The same test asserts card_size <= CARD_LIMIT for review_impl, which the design's own text makes impossible: review_impl is 3,948 bytes on read_dev in this world, and 4,219 bytes after shrink once the design's section 2 instruction, the review sentence and the four instruction listings are added (scratch copy; design 3,134, review_design 3,985, adversary_design 3,699). The new instruction view adds about 270 bytes that no existing shrink step can recover, and design section 9 already allows a review card above the target. Implement could pass only by changing fixed instruction text or adding shrink steps the design lacks. Fix: keep the limit for design, review_design and adversary_design; for review_impl assert growth of at most one view reference over the card without the instruction (or no limit), and note that design section 10 test 1 is relaxed for review_impl as section 9 allows.

The approve-item node set conflicts with OpDecisionTests: section 5 and D5 say approve items (and the PR body) read human_decisions over the item's ancestor nodes, but in the shipped graph integrate is not an ancestor of approve_merge (its ancestors are adversary_design, approve_design, base, design, filter_design, filter_impl, implement, review_design, review_impl, review_tests, run_tests, test_design), nor of itself for the PR body, and merge is an op. Under the rule an answered integrate question is shown nowhere, contrary to section 1 step 5 ('approve_merge and the PR body list every answered question') and D5/revision 3 (op questions appear in the list). test_an_answered_integrate_question_is_listed_with_kind_op asserts it on approve_merge, so an implementation following section 5 fails a frozen test and one passing it departs from the design. State the node set (for example, for approve_merge every graph node except its descendants, or ancestors plus the op nodes beside it; and whether the PR body includes integrate's own answers), then align the test.

output.summary: Tests cover the journey, the blocked/answered/stale cases, review and filter cards, the shrink step and the prompts, and fail only for the missing feature; but test 1 cannot pass (abandon makes the reviews reclaimable; review_impl measures 4,219 bytes with the design's text), and the design's ancestor rule leaves integrate's op answer off approve_merge, which a frozen test requires.

spec:
The owner's feedback (2026-11-01): "I noticed you haven't asked me for much input on design... for this release branching goal I would have expected to be grilled." Approvals stay delegated ("I did delegate my approval to you, I don't think we need machinery around that"). What is missing is the interview. Today `design` goes straight from the spec to a document, and an agent told not to wait decides the owner's choices itself. G1025 (release branching) was designed that way until the root interviewed the owner by hand, and four of its decisions changed.

The owner's mechanism, verbatim: "during design review, gaps that the human needs to answer should be flagged in the review, and that would stale the design, and require interview to fix it." Build it from existing parts:
1. Review side: the shared review instruction (and the design reviewer's prompt) says: raise a finding whose text starts `owner question:` (question, options, recommendation) only for an owner's choice as defined below. The owner's follow-up, verbatim: "we shouldn't have to bother the user for every detail. I think the way we previously judged this was using the concept of bounded scope i.e. decisions that have big consequences should be asked." The owner rejected the old definition: "we don't need to continue that previous definition, goal-sized seems very vague tbh". The test instead: if this choice turned out wrong, what would undoing it touch? If the undo stays inside this goal's own change, the choice is the designer's. If it reaches anything outside it (other goals that build on it; users' repositories or installed policy; stored records or formats; names or outputs others consume such as CLI output, branch names and config keys; external systems), or the choice changes what the product does for its users or the project's direction, it is the owner's, unless one option clearly dominates. A choice whose undo stays inside the goal, or one where an option clearly dominates, stays the designer's and is recorded with its reasoning; a reviewer who disagrees with it raises an ordinary finding. Such owner-question findings are always material, so the filter cannot demote them. Write this test once (a short reference the prompts cite) rather than repeating it in each prompt.
2. Design side: design.md says to answer an `owner question:` correction by submitting `--blocked` (waiting_for human) with that question, the options and the recommendation, never by deciding it. The existing blocked human item, `answer` and the retry card's `answer` carry the owner's words back. The revised design records them verbatim as owner decisions and answers the finding `fixed: owner chose …`.
3. Display (the only engine change, if any): approve_design and approve_merge items and the PR body list the owner questions with the owner's answers, so a delegated approval still shows what the owner decided.
4. The execute skill tells the root to batch owner questions across goals so the owner answers several in one sitting.
5. Approval delegation is unchanged. A design with no owner questions costs nothing extra.

Acceptance:
- Card snapshots show the owner-question instruction on design-review cards and in design.md.
- An engine journey test: a review raises an `owner question:` finding; design reopens and submits --blocked; the human item appears; the answer reaches the retry card; the design resubmits and the review approves; approve_design lists the question and the answer.
- The filter test shows an `owner question:` note is promoted or refused as non-material (decide in the design).
- The execute skill documents batching.
- This PR edits docs/design for its contract changes and adds a HISTORY §4 row (G1017's rule).
title: Design review flags owner questions; the design blocks for an interview to answer them
